svg.title: Figure 2. Four changes that closed the public network case, and what is left of it
svg.desc: Four developments that removed most of the original argument for using a VPN on an untrusted network. Encrypted web traffic became near universal, exceeding ninety five percent of page loads. Preloaded strict transport security means browsers refuse plaintext for major sites, so downgrade attacks fail. Encrypted domain name lookups stopped the query leaking to the local network. And encrypted client hello, standardised in March 2026, hides the server name in the handshake, which was the last thing left in clear text. A band below lists what genuinely remains, and a final band gives the reasons to use a VPN that are still sound, none of which is the coffee shop.
svg.text: Figure 2: The Coffee Shop Case Has Largely Expired
"Always use a VPN on public wireless" was excellent advice in 2013. Four things happened since, and standard guidance has not noticed the fourth.

g.text: list of sites they will only
Free, built in, and it needs
The last thing in clear text

svg.text: What genuinely remains, stated without exaggeration

g.text: The addresses you connect to. Still visible to the local network, though shared hosting means one address often serves many sites, which blunts it considerably.
Timing and volume. When you are online and how much you move. A VPN hides the destinations and not this, so it is a partial answer at best.
Coverage gaps. The fourth item needs encrypted DNS and a supporting host, so it is not yet everywhere. Older or badly maintained sites still fall short on the first.
A genuinely hostile network can still refuse to route you, or serve a captive portal that asks for things. Neither is fixed by a tunnel it will not let you open.

svg.text: The reasons to use a VPN that are still sound, and none of them is the coffee shop

g.text: You would rather the provider had your browsing than your network operator. A real preference, especially where operators may sell it. Figure 1 is the whole argument.
Reaching something your network blocks. Censorship, geography, or a restrictive corporate or campus network. This works, when the tunnel itself is not blocked.
Not showing a target your home address. The professional case, during authorised work. Lesson 5.2's point about your movements being engagement data applies here too.

svg.text: Notice that all three surviving reasons are about who sees your traffic or where it appears to come from. None is about interception.
Which means the honest recommendation is narrower than "always on public wireless", and considerably easier to justify to somebody who asks why.
The bad version of this advice survives because it is simple, and because the people repeating it are often selling the subscription.
